items.title: Tracking Down a Mystery Beep By Giving a Coding Agent a Few Ears
items.summary: [Simon Willison] recently used a coding agent in an unusual way. A software system temporarily used the microphones on devices scattered around the room to triangulate the source of a mysterious, intermittent beep coming from within one of the many boxes in the room. The main part of the system is a Python web server, and the listeners can be any old devices one might have hanging around. Scan a QR code, and the device becomes a listening post by leveraging the Web Audio API. With listeners spread around the room, the system has everything it needs to patiently wait, listen, and zero in on the mystery beep. The culprit? An old carbon monoxide detector, buried in a box and emitting a low battery chirp. That’s neat, but what this project really demonstrates is the benefit of hacking together a way for a coding agent to actually sense the real world, the better for it to design a solution to a physical problem. The ad-hoc framework of web-based listeners allowed [Simon] to give the agent the ability to gather audio data on its own to refine and recalibrate its approach during development, without any need for him to record audio and pass it on manually. It’s a bit reminiscent of this WiFi analyzer connected to an AI model , a project that hints at the possibilities of a physical tool that can be steered by an agent. Check out the GitHub repository for beep-locator if you’d like a closer look at the code itself. Imagine sitting there typing in a prompt to find the beep. items.summary: You could read manga in the classic bound paper format. But then you’d have to carry around lots of volumes that take up lots of space. items.title: Handheld Motor Cancels Out Every Twist and Turn
items.summary: It’s one thing to know that input from a motion sensor can steer a motor. It’s another to see and feel the two cancelling out the other in real-time, right in the palm of one’s hand. That’s [cpietsch]’s takeaway from the CAN do GYRO , a brushless motor with a CAN interface and tiny STM32-based development board perched atop it. It’s essentially a one-axis gimbal with a few thoughtful features. The unit tracks itself fully in three dimensions, so while the motor is limited to one axis, the unit doesn’t get confused by complex movements. It also auto-calibrates, and auto-stops within half a rotation if it detects the motor spinning freely. The hardware consists of a tiny XIAO STM32C5 microcontroller board with integrated IMU (Inertial Measurement Unit) and CAN transceiver, and an M5Stack RollerCAN motor. The motor, handily, has a small OLED screen built into it. Combined with a battery it’s small enough to be handheld while it shows off what a tight control loop paired with a suitable motor can do. Watch it in action in the video, embedded below. Of course, accurate gimbals using brushless motors have been around for many years. But one thing that’s plain is just how much the kind of hardware available to individuals has changed. Compare this build to a DIY gimbal project from about ten years ago and you’ll see the function looks about the same, but today’s hardware has evolved considerably. items.title: Serial: The Port That Won’t Die
items.summary: Computers have changed quite a bit over the last 60 years. Good luck plugging in an old MFM disk into your modern computer. Plugging in a parallel printer is difficult, although not impossible, as long as the device really is a printer. But the humble serial port refuses to die. Sure, you probably don’t have a 25-pin connector on your laptop anymore. You might not even have a nine-pin connector. But serial communication is everywhere, especially if you work with microcontrollers or industrial equipment. The connectors have changed, but much of the underlying technology would be recognizable to someone working with a computer in 1975. The ASR-33 was the best way to talk to a computer until it wasn’t. (Photo by [ArnoldReinhold] CC-BY-SA-3.0) Before video terminals, there were teletypes. These electromechanical beasts could send and receive characters over wires using a current loop. Older machines, such as the Teletype Models 15 and 28, commonly used 60 mA loops (and five-bit codes), often at 120 volts DC. Later machines, including the iconic ASR-33, generally used 20 mA loops. Current flowing represented a mark, while an interruption in the current represented a space. Marks and spaces on the line translate to 1s and 0s. The beauty of current loops was their simplicity, relative resistance to electrical noise, and their ability to drive very long cables. The Electronic Industries Association introduced RS-232 in 1960, followed by RS-232A in 1963 and RS-232B in 1965. The familiar RS-232C arrived in 1969, followed by revisions D, E, and F. You’ll also see EIA-232 and TIA-232, but everyone still calls it RS-232. Unlike ordinary logic signals, RS-232 uses positive and negative voltages. Determined to find out what was inhabiting his local electromagnetic spectrum, [Tommy] picked up a cheap RTL-SDR receiver and an antenna. The goal? Receiving some ISS image transmissions. The results? Let’s say mixed . But it lit a fire, and soon, he had more hardware than he could handle on his own. The slope became slippery, and before he knew it, the Starlab Observatory was an Open Source GitHub Project ! What makes it an Observatory instead of a random menagerie of radio memorabilia? Intelligence. An ESP32 based antenna switch takes commands from a dedicated Ubuntu computer. The PC, running Starlab , predicts satellite passes, and selects the correct receiver and antenna combination to receive data, which then gets logged and processed. Multiple jobs can run at once.
